# CHAPTER 492

## THE RESPONDENT

The morning after drinking with Antonius, somebody knocked on the door hard enough to make my head object on principle.

Not pain.

Just criticism.

Two small beers had apparently left behind one dry mouth, one slower first thought, and a powerful belief that doors should be quieter before breakfast.

Lyssa was already awake.

Of course.

She sat at the table with dark cloth spread across her lap and three pins held between her lips.

I had one blanket over my legs and no moral authority.

The knock came again.

Lyssa looked at me.

I looked at the door.

She raised one eyebrow.

"I am recovering."

She removed the pins.

"From walking home?"

"Social activity."

"Open the door."

Cruel household government.

I put both crutches under me and stood.

Body fine.

Right shoulder ordinary.

Residual limb ordinary.

No strange skin complaint.

Only mouth dry enough that swallowing felt administrative.

I crossed the room.

The person outside was not Antonius.

Good.

One chapter of voluntary friendship-adjacent behavior was enough pressure for civilization.

It was a district runner.

Not Carrow district colors exactly.

Blue strip on gray shoulder.

Travel pouch.

Flat document case.

He looked at me.

Then at the folded paper in his hand.

"Gregory?"

"Depends."

"Gregory of Carrow, temporary route witness and commercial screener?"

That was worse.

"Yes."

He held out the paper.

"Lakeward administrative relay. Receipt requested."

There it was.

Lakeward.

My brain became sober immediately.

Not fully.

Enough.

I took the paper.

Did not open it yet.

"What kind of relay?"

"I carry it. I don't interpret it."

Excellent profession.

He produced a little receipt slip.

My name.

Origin mark.

Carrow delivery line.

Nothing saying arrest, fine, charge, complaint, summons, execution, or congratulations on successful regional smuggling.

Promising.

"Sign here?"

"If you're Gregory."

"I am increasingly sure."

I signed.

He checked it.

"Response instructions are inside if response is required."

"That sounds ominous."

"People say that about every letter."

"Are they usually right?"

"I carry them."

Right.

He left.

I closed the door.

Lyssa had stopped sewing.

That was evidence.

Not proof of concern.

She looked at the folded paper.

"Lakeward?"

"Yes."

"Work?"

"Maybe."

Bad answer.

I looked at the seal again.

Not merchant-house.

Not field office I recognized.

Lakeward district mark with smaller stamp beneath.

**HERITAGE RELEASE / RECORD RECONCILIATION**

Oh.

There it was.

I knew exactly one reason that office might know my name.

The gray freight.

My mouth became drier without help from beer.

Lyssa watched my face.

"Not work."

"Probably not."

"Greg."

"I am opening it."

I sat before doing that.

No reason to perform standing anxiety when chair existed.

The document was three sheets.

First page formal.

Second page questions.

Third page return instructions.

I read the first page once too fast.

Then again like Hessa had been hiding behind my shoulder.

**LAKEWARD DISTRICT HERITAGE RELEASE OFFICE**

**REQUEST FOR FACTUAL STATEMENT**

**POST-SALE RELEASE RECONCILIATION / PRE-MERGER ROUTE HARDWARE**

Not summons.

Not charge.

Request.

Keep reading.

The office was reconciling a municipal surplus sale involving pre-merger route hardware later presented outside district without prior export release.

One marked lot had apparently been returned to Lakeward jurisdiction for release review.

Returned by whom?

Not stated.

Current owner?

Not stated.

The office had municipal sale records, Cinder Cross intake records, and a buyer notation identifying me as an external screener present when the marked lot was examined.

There.

The buyer.

Of course he wrote things down.

Functional people were dangerous like that.

The letter said my statement was requested to establish **observed custody, markings, disclosed knowledge, and condition at examination**.

It explicitly said:

**Do not provide legal conclusion unless personally qualified.**

Beautiful.

I almost liked them.

Then the next line:

**A factual response does not waive any district authority concerning persons, property, release status, transport, penalty, or later inquiry.**

There we go.

Less beautiful.

Lyssa said, "What is it?"

I kept reading.

Questions.

One: Were you present when municipal surplus route hardware was transported from Lakeward toward Cinder Cross?

Yes.

Two: Did you review sale records before transport?

Yes.

Three: Did those records appear to identify municipal sale of the transported lots?

Yes, with limits.

Four: Before departure, were you aware that any pre-merger route-hardware lot lacked district export release?

Yes.

There.

No clever wording available.

Five: Did you personally conceal, alter, remove, forge, or destroy a release mark, ownership mark, sale record, crate seal, inventory entry, or inspection record?

No.

Six: Did you instruct another person to do so?

No.

Seven: At Cinder Cross, did you identify any piece as Three Rays marked or compatible?

One piece as Three Rays marked.

Compatibility for others uncertain.

Eight: Was the marked lot purchased by the Cinder Cross buyer?

No.

Nine: What was the last custody state you personally observed?

Marked lot remained with seller after buyer refused current purchase without release or deeper discount.

Ten: Do you know current location?

No.

Eleven: Do you know original removal site or whether hardware was ever removed unlawfully from an active route?

No.

Twelve: Were you compensated in connection with transport or sale?

Yes.

Ah.

There was the eight silver.

No reason to hide it.

Reason to dislike writing it.

Lyssa said, "Greg."

I put the paper down.

"I did something illegal in Lakeward."

Silence.

Good opening.

Maybe not.

Lyssa set the cloth aside.

Not dramatically.

Carefully, because pins.

"How illegal?"

Useful question.

"Export paperwork illegal. Not stolen-goods illegal by what I knew."

"By what you knew."

"Yes."

She waited.

The converged version of me lasted longer than five seconds.

Not much longer.

"Municipal surplus," I said. "Road hardware. Two lots had pre-merger export controls. Seller had bought them legally from Lakeward district, at least according to sale receipts that matched the lots. She had not gotten the separate release stamp before moving them east. Waiting for release would have missed her buyer window."

Lyssa looked at the letter.

"You knew."

"Yes."

No defense.

That felt worse and better.

"Before you went?"

"Before we left Lakeward."

"And you went anyway."

"Yes."

She leaned back.

Not angry enough to perform anger.

More like fitting a new piece into an old pattern she had not requested.

"Why?"

That one had several answers.

Ride east.

Money.

The stock appeared legitimately owned.

The release rule looked badly applied to old warehouse junk.

The buyer window.

Curiosity.

Confidence.

A little criminal nostalgia probably deserved no daylight.

"Because the property looked legitimately purchased, the release rule looked administrative rather than protecting somebody from immediate harm, and the pay made the risk real."

"How much?"

"Eight silver plus the ride after the marked lot failed. Twelve if whole load had sold."

Her eyebrows moved.

Not because eight silver was impossible money anymore.

Because I had omitted an eight-silver illegal job from the travel report.

"You told me about glass."

"Yes."

"You told me about the shoulder."

"Yes."

"You told me about the road."

"Yes."

"You did not tell me this."

"No."

There.

No clever version.

She looked at the letter again.

"Was anyone else taking the risk without knowing?"

That surprised me.

Then it didn't.

Practical.

"Driver knew the release was missing. Seller was paying ordinary rate. I made her negotiate a risk premium with him before I agreed."

"Made?"

"Refused my part until she did. Driver asked four silver. She paid four."

"Good."

Not absolution.

Just one fact landing where it belonged.

"Were the things stolen?"

"I saw municipal sale receipts. Lot numbers matched. No active-road removal in the sale record. I do not know where the district got them before the warehouse sale."

"So you don't know."

"Correct."

"Did you lie at the gate?"

That one was uglier.

"Not directly."

Her face changed.

"Greg."

"The load was listed as retired repair stock. That was true and incomplete. Clerk asked about charged glass and active signal parts. Seller answered no. Nobody asked whether pre-merger release was missing. I had already told seller that if anyone asked me directly, I would answer. Nobody did."

Lyssa stared at me.

"That is lawyer-shaped."

"Yes."

"Were you a lawyer?"

"No."

"Then don't."

Fair.

"I knowingly let incomplete paperwork carry the load through."

"Better."

"Worse legally."

"Better sentence."

Also fair.

I picked the letter up again.

"They aren't asking me to decide law. They want factual statement."

"Will you answer?"

Immediate instinct: yes.

Second instinct: ask what answering exposed.

Third: maybe I should find somebody who understood district procedure.

That did not mean Antonius.

Absolutely not Antonius the morning after beer.

Also he was not automatically my lawyer because he owned ledgers aggressively.

I read the return instructions.

Statement could be returned through Carrow district relay within twelve days.

Signature had to be witnessed by a district clerk, registered notary, licensed advocate, or magistrate-office clerk.

No appearance in Lakeward required unless later ordered.

Voluntary factual response.

Failure to respond could leave the record unresolved but was not itself listed as offense.

Interesting.

"I think yes," I said.

Lyssa nodded once.

"Think?"

"I want somebody local to tell me what `voluntary factual response` actually does before I sign it. Not what happened. I know what happened. What signing means procedurally."

"That sounds less stupid."

"Growth."

"Don't celebrate yet."

Hostile household again.

I ate bread.

Drank water.

Then read the questions a third time.

No need to rush to district office with yesterday's beer still arguing quietly with my body.

By second bell I felt normal enough to stop thinking about it.

We went separately.

Lyssa had work.

That mattered.

She did not come supervise my administrative consequences.

Before leaving she said, "Tell me what they say."

"Yes."

"Actual words."

"Cruel."

"Greg."

"Actual words."

Carrow district relay office sat near the records quarter where every building looked like it had been designed by someone who believed windows encouraged fraud.

I had used the place for route receipts before.

Never as a respondent.

Title acquired.

Great.

The front clerk was an older man with a narrow beard and no interest in my internal development.

Perfect.

I showed the Lakeward letter.

"I want to know what this response does before I submit it."

He read the header.

"Heritage release reconciliation."

"Yes."

"You need legal advice?"

"I need to know whether your office can tell me what the process means without telling me what I should say."

He looked at me over the paper.

"Better question."

I was collecting those.

He pointed to a side desk.

"Records clerk can explain relay and witness function. Legal advice is advocate."

Good.

Different authority.

The records clerk was a woman with square spectacles and six piles of paper arranged by a system I wanted to ask about but valued survival.

She read the return page.

"Voluntary means Lakeward requested it without current order compelling you to answer."

"If I answer, does Carrow decide whether it's true?"

"No. We witness signature and identity only."

"Does witness mean you certify content?"

"No."

"Does sending it waive anything?"

She tapped the sentence that already said it did not waive district authority.

"Not according to this form. I am not giving you broader legal advice."

"Good."

"If you want advice about exposure, hire advocate."

There.

Money question.

I had twelve silver-ish reserve.

Not poverty.

Also no reason to spend silver reflexively if the form only asked facts I already intended to state honestly.

Still, knowingly participating in controlled-export movement was not nothing.

"What does a short review usually cost?"

"Ask an advocate."

Right.

I left district office without signing.

That felt responsible enough to be suspicious.

There were three licensed advocates within two streets according to posted board.

One handled family/property disputes.

One commercial claims.

One transport and municipal licensing.

Useful specificity.

I chose transport.

Not because destiny.

Because sign.

The advocate's front room had two benches, one clerk, and a wall map with colored route strips pinned over it.

The clerk read my letter.

"Document review only?"

"I want to know what answering factually exposes or changes. I am not asking anyone to invent a defense before I know whether I need one."

"Consult fee three copper."

That was almost comforting.

Not silver.

Not everything had to scale because my purse did.

I paid.

Three copper could be three copper.

The advocate was a woman named Irena Voss according to the plate on her desk.

Name established by furniture.

Excellent provenance.

She read the Lakeward request without speaking.

Then the questions.

Then looked at me.

"Did you know release was missing?"

"Yes."

"Before transport?"

"Yes."

"Did you own the goods?"

"No."

"Drive?"

"No."

"Arrange original sale?"

"No."

"Remove marks?"

"No."

"Alter paperwork?"

"No."

"Get paid?"

"Yes."

"For transport?"

"Screening and helping preserve sale. Ride included."

"Amount?"

"Eight silver after partial acceptance. Twelve would have been full-load acceptance."

She paused at that.

Not judgment.

Scale.

"What did you actually do during transport?"

I described it.

Reviewed receipts.

Compared lots.

Confirmed release missing.

Refused involvement until driver negotiated risk premium.

Rode with load.

Did not open sealed crates.

Did not lie when asked nothing useful.

That sentence got corrected immediately.

"Do not say it that way."

"Lyssa already objected."

"Lyssa is correct."

Disease spreading.

"Say what happened. Do not turn omission into a legal theory."

"Fine."

At Cinder Cross, seller and buyer opened lots.

I identified one Three Rays mark.

Buyer rejected marked lot because missing release created resale/capital risk.

Seller retained it.

I was paid partial fee.

Last saw marked lot with seller.

No current location.

No original removal provenance.

Irena read question four again.

"Your truthful answer is yes."

"Yes."

"That answer may be against your interest if Lakeward later examines transport liability."

"I assumed."

"But refusing now does not erase Cinder records identifying you."

"Also assumed."

"Do not assume legal consequences."

Right.

"What would you do?"

She looked at me.

"You are paying for advice, so I will answer. Based only on this letter and your account, I would respond narrowly, truthfully, and without volunteering legal conclusions or motives. You have documentary facts that may help establish lawful municipal ownership and later custody. You also have a fact that may expose knowing participation in export without release. Both can be true."

There.

Observation could be real while attribution remained unsettled.

Annoying when my own system turned around and bit me.

"Should I explain why I thought the release rule was stupid here?"

"No."

Fast.

"Why?"

"Because they did not ask whether you approved of the rule."

Good.

"Should I explain driver premium?"

"Question twelve asks compensation in connection with transport or sale. If you mention your own compensation, and driver premium is relevant to what you were paid to do, maybe. But do not write a moral essay proving everyone consented."

"I hate how accurately you predicted the essay."

"Common problem."

"Greg problem."

"I have known you eleven minutes."

Fair.

We drafted nothing together.

Important.

She told me process and risk.

My statement remained mine.

I went back to district office with four pages in notebook first.

Too many.

Cut them.

Three pages.

Still too many.

The records clerk watched me cross out half a paragraph.

"Need desk?"

"Apparently."

She pointed to one.

I wrote the statement cleanly.

No story.

No defense.

No apology.

No cleverness.

Just sequence.

**I was present before and during transport from Lakeward toward Cinder Cross.**

**I reviewed municipal sale records presented by the seller. The lot numbers I checked matched the transported inventory. I did not independently verify the district's chain before municipal sale.**

**Before departure I knew two pre-merger route-hardware lots lacked export release.**

That line looked ugly.

Stayed.

**I did not alter, remove, forge, conceal, or destroy any release mark, ownership mark, sale record, crate seal, inventory entry, or inspection record, and I did not instruct another person to do so.**

**At Cinder Cross the owner and buyer opened the relevant lot. I identified one toothed arc bearing a Three Rays mark. I described other pieces only as possibly compatible where I was not certain.**

**The buyer declined current purchase of the marked route lot without release or a larger discount. The seller retained that lot. That is the last custody state I personally observed. I do not know its current location.**

**I do not know the original removal site or whether any piece was unlawfully removed from an active route before municipal sale.**

**I was compensated eight silver plus transport after the buyer accepted the clean remainder and rejected the marked lot. My agreed compensation would have been twelve silver plus transport if the buyer accepted the full load.**

Then one extra sentence.

I stared at it before deciding.

**Before I agreed to participate, I confirmed the driver knew the release was absent; the driver separately negotiated a four-silver risk premium with the seller.**

Relevant?

Maybe.

It established disclosed knowledge among participants, not innocence.

Question: disclosed knowledge.

Keep.

No statement that this made transport acceptable.

No statement that law was stupid.

No statement that nobody was harmed.

I did not know that.

The records clerk read only enough to check blank spaces and identity line.

"Content is yours."

"Good."

"Sign in front of me."

I did.

She witnessed name and date.

Stamped relay receipt.

"Lakeward copy leaves afternoon packet."

"Can I keep exact copy?"

"You should."

Of course.

She made one.

I paid copy fee in bits.

Ordinary money.

No ceremony.

Outside, I stood on the records-office step with two crutches and one document proving I had voluntarily told a district office that yes, I knowingly participated in moving export-controlled hardware without the required release.

This was not how I imagined financial independence feeling.

Good.

Probably healthier.

I walked home.

Lyssa was not there.

Also good.

Her life had continued during my administrative suspense.

Dark cloth gone from table.

One cup upside down by basin.

Someone downstairs arguing about onions.

I put my copy in the household records place.

Not hidden.

Not displayed like trophy.

Just with papers.

Then I waited badly for about half a bell before realizing waiting for Lyssa to return had become another form of filling silence.

So I ate.

Repaired one loose wrap on crutch handle.

Checked my notebook.

Did not invent a Lakeward outcome.

Did not calculate fines nobody had named.

Did not decide the marked lot had become historically important because an office cared about release.

Administrative attention was not value proof.

It was administrative attention.

Lyssa came back with thread wrapped around one wrist and a paper bundle under her arm.

She saw me.

Then the records copy beside my notebook.

"You answered."

"Yes."

She set her bundle down.

"What did they say? Actual words."

Right.

I told her about the district clerk.

Witness certifies signature, not content.

Voluntary means requested without current order compelling response.

Legal advice separate.

Three-copper advocate review.

Irena saying both facts could be true: municipal ownership might be supported and I might still have knowingly joined transport without release.

Lyssa nodded.

"That sounds true."

"Annoying theme."

"What did you write?"

I handed her the copy.

She read slower than Antonius but faster than me pretending not to watch.

At the eight-silver line, her finger stopped.

Then moved.

At the driver premium, stopped again.

Then end.

"You really knew."

"Yes."

"And you really made sure he knew."

"Yes."

"Those don't cancel."

"I know."

She handed it back.

"Good."

I waited.

"Good what?"

"Good answer."

"Not good crime."

"No."

There.

Enough.

She picked up her bundle again.

"What happens now?"

"I don't know."

"Can they fine you?"

"Possibly. Advocate wouldn't guess without Lakeward rule and actual role classification."

"Can they make you go back?"

"Not from this letter. Later maybe if ordered."

"Are you going to tell Antonius?"

I thought about that.

Yesterday I had almost told him accidentally.

Today the fact had moved.

It was not only mine anymore because Lyssa knew and Lakeward had my signed statement.

That did not create a duty to give Antonius every gray thing in my life.

"Not automatically."

Lyssa nodded.

No demand.

Good.

"If this becomes money or court or business problem, probably. If not, he doesn't need confession because we had beer once."

"Good."

Two goods in one afternoon.

Dangerous.

She opened her bundle.

Thread.

Of course.

Dark blue.

Two shades so similar I immediately refused participation.

"Which one?" she asked.

"No."

She smiled.

"Growth."

"I have legal counsel now."

"Three copper made you unbearable."

"Excellent return."

She went back to work.

I sat across from her.

Lakeward existed several roads away with my statement traveling toward it.

The marked Three Rays lot existed somewhere I could not currently prove.

The seller might have brought it back for release.

The buyer might have written exactly enough notes to create this whole problem.

Some clerk might decide nothing else mattered.

Some other clerk might decide I owed money.

None of those were facts yet.

For once, I let them stay that way.

I had answered the question I actually had.

That was enough for today.
# CHAPTER 493

## THE CLIENT

The letter from Duskport arrived three days after I told Lakeward exactly how stupid I had been on purpose.

That was good timing.

Not emotionally.

Administratively.

Lakeward could keep deciding whether I had become expensive paperwork. I had already answered the question in front of me.

Hark & Venn had apparently found a different one.

The packet runner caught me on the stairs.

"Greg?"

"Yes."

"Duskport."

He handed me a folded sheet with a workshop stamp I recognized before I read the name.

HARK & VENN.

My entire left side became interested.

Not magic.

Body.

Different system.

I signed receipt.

The runner left.

I stood on the landing with two crutches, one sealed letter, and the sudden urge to open it with my teeth.

I did not.

Hands existed.

Use them.

Upstairs, Lyssa had half our table occupied with a gray coat turned inside out. One sleeve was pinned flat. The other looked like it had lost an argument with chalk.

She glanced at the letter.

"Duskport?"

"Yes."

"Hark and Venn?"

I looked at her.

"How?"

"You made that face."

"I have multiple faces."

"You have purchase face, road face, Hessa face, and leg shop face."

"This is profiling."

"Open it."

Hostile household government remained stable.

I sat.

The seal came apart cleanly.

Inside was one page.

Masta's handwriting had not improved.

Good.

Some institutions survived distance.

**GREG.**

Excellent opening.

**NEXT SOCKET SHELL READY FOR SECOND FIT. TEMPORARY ASH SHAFT AND MEDIUM TEST FOOT RETAINED HERE. BRING LINER. DO NOT PAY ANYTHING YET. QUOTE UNCHANGED.**

I read that line twice.

No payment due.

Good.

Not because I could not pay.

Because paying without reason was still stupid.

Progress.

The next lines:

**I HAVE FITTING SPACE SIX DAYS FROM RECEIPT, THIRD BELL THROUGH FIFTH. IF YOU CANNOT MAKE THAT WINDOW, SEND WORD. I WILL GIVE ANOTHER. NOTHING EXPIRES BECAUSE YOU HAVE A LIFE.**

I looked at Lyssa.

"She knows me too well."

Lyssa held out a hand.

I gave her the letter.

She read.

Then the last part.

Her mouth changed.

Small.

Trying not to smile.

"What?"

She turned the page toward me.

I had not reached bottom.

**BRING ONE REAL TASK YOU WANT TWO HANDS FOR. NOT STANDING THERE FEELING IMPORTANT.**

I stared.

"Rude."

"Very specific."

"I stood for one second."

"You told everyone."

"I had hands."

"You currently have hands."

"While standing."

She gave letter back.

I read the line again.

Real task.

Not demonstration.

Not walking for walking.

Not standing there feeling important.

Masta remained Masta.

Good.

I put the letter beside Lakeward copy.

Two papers.

One said I had knowingly joined a controlled-export problem.

One said a new socket shell existed six days away.

Life had range.

Lyssa returned to coat.

No immediate speech.

Good.

I tried same.

Lasted maybe thirty seconds.

"Six days."

"Yes."

"Duskport."

"Also yes."

"I could make that."

She pulled one pin out and moved it half inch.

"Probably."

"I need route."

"Then get route."

There was something insulting about living with someone who refused to turn every decision into event.

Useful.

I went to the travel board after breakfast.

Not work board.

That distinction took effort.

Carrow had three ways east that mattered.

Passenger coach.

Freight passage.

Packet carriage with spare seat if clerk liked your face or your paperwork.

Old Greg would have optimized.

Current Greg also wanted to optimize.

Disease survived reincarnation.

Passenger board showed a Duskport connection leaving tomorrow morning, one overnight stop, then direct east after second bell.

Fare: one silver, three copper.

Food not included.

Return not included.

I stared at price.

Not because impossible.

Because possible.

That was new enough to need a second look.

One silver, three copper did not threaten rent.

Did not threaten food.

Did not threaten Hark & Venn final balance.

Did not threaten Vale because Vale was dead.

Beautiful sentence.

It did reduce reserve.

Real money.

Not ceremonial.

Freight board had cheaper options.

Of course.

**EAST HARDWARE / RIDER ACCEPTED / LOAD + UNLOAD / DUSKPORT TERMINAL / TWO COPPER + WORK**

There.

Old friend.

Cheap travel disguised as labor.

My shoulder was fine.

Hands fine.

Could load.

Probably.

Another listing:

**MAIL AUXILIARY / EAST / NIGHT DEPARTURE / ONE BIT / NO GUARANTEED SEAT**

Tempting.

Awful.

Then:

**TIMBER WAGON / DUSKPORT OUTER YARD / PASSAGE FREE WITH TWO DAYS STACKING**

No.

Not because stacking beneath me.

Because Hark & Venn wanted body information, and arriving after two days of timber work would change the body I brought to the fitting.

That mattered.

I looked back at passenger fare.

One silver, three copper.

Paying money to arrive in a useful condition.

Annoying concept.

I had spent months treating travel like something work should subsidize.

Sometimes rational.

Sometimes cheap because I was broke.

Sometimes cheap because I enjoyed making logistics prove affection.

The clerk behind window looked at me.

"Buying?"

"Thinking."

"Do it farther left."

A woman behind me wanted board.

Fair.

I moved.

Sat on stone bench.

Did arithmetic without conversion.

Twelve silver-ish reserve.

Ordinary copper and bits.

One silver, three copper outbound.

Food.

Lodging included at connection? Board said no.

Fine.

Return later.

Final limb balance still future.

No Vale.

No current fine from Lakeward.

No new contract.

The old version of me would have turned uncertainty into reason to preserve every coin.

The even older version would have said money existed to remove friction and bought whatever was fastest.

Both men were annoying.

I read freight listing again.

Two copper plus work.

Could save nearly a silver-scale chunk.

Could also arrive with shoulder fatigue, hand soreness, and whatever stacking did to residual-limb volume after long standing.

Then Masta would spend fitting time separating travel labor from socket problems.

Bad experiment.

There.

Hessa disease.

Again.

I hated cross-domain lessons.

I bought passenger ticket.

One silver, three copper.

The clerk took money without music.

No achievement.

No one nearby understood that I had just paid not to work.

Excellent.

Ticket folded into notebook.

Then I bought return option?

No.

I almost did.

Stopped.

I did not know how long fitting would take.

Masta might want another next day.

Might say go home.

Might need adjustment.

Buying return schedule before shop told me current state would be me inventing future to feel organized.

I kept money.

Restraint.

Disgusting.

Back home, Lyssa had changed coats.

Not physically.

Different garment now on table.

Brown cuff.

I recognized it because it had survived more chapters than some governments.

I put ticket down.

"Passenger coach."

She looked.

"Work ride full?"

"No."

"Bad route?"

"No."

"Then why?"

"I paid."

She stopped.

"You paid passenger fare?"

"Yes."

"Without trying to earn it back on the way?"

"Yes."

She looked suspicious.

"This legal letter changed you."

"Temporary condition."

"How much?"

"One silver, three copper."

She winced slightly.

Good.

Not nothing.

"Why not freight?"

I told her.

Two days stacking.

Body state.

Fitting data.

She nodded.

"That makes sense."

I hated how much I wanted praise for basic resource allocation.

Did not ask.

Training.

"Leaving tomorrow?"

"Yes."

"How long?"

"I don't know."

She resumed stitching.

"Good."

"Good?"

"You usually tell me a return date you invented."

I opened mouth.

Closed.

Damn.

"Need anything from Duskport?" I asked.

"No."

"Thread?"

"No."

"Needles?"

"No."

"Glass blue line thing?"

She looked up.

"No."

"Great. Efficient."

"Come back with your own leg problem."

"Technically socket."

"Greg."

"Yes."

That was enough.

Packing took less time than expected.

Also progress.

Crutches.

Bag.

Notebook.

Money separated.

Lakeward copy stayed home.

No reason to carry it east like a worry charm.

Liner.

Important.

I almost forgot liner.

That would have been embarrassing enough to justify religion.

Lyssa saw me stop halfway down stairs.

"What?"

"Liner."

She pointed upward.

"You put it beside bed."

"Yes."

I went back.

Tavi was in lower room building something from four sticks and a bent spoon.

He looked at liner in my hand.

"Leg?"

"Part of leg."

"New?"

"Old part. New shell."

"Can you run?"

"No."

"Can you kick?"

"Probably badly."

"Can you jump?"

"Absolutely not."

He considered.

"What can it do?"

That was fair.

I looked at the liner.

Then letter.

"Maybe let me stand and use both hands longer."

He looked unimpressed.

Children had terrible product instincts.

"What will you do with hands?"

There.

Masta's question through smaller mouth.

Real task.

I had been thinking about it badly.

Carry something.

Use tool.

Open door.

Write while standing?

Not useful enough.

Old Greg could fight with both hands.

Current Greg did not need a sword demonstration in prosthetic shop.

I thought about South Road.

Clipboard.

Not both hands.

West Market.

Records.

Again.

Theatre.

Props.

Could carry.

Lyssa work.

Not mine.

Kitchen.

Pot.

Interesting.

At home, using crutches meant any object larger than bag became route problem.

Cup from table to stove.

Bowl.

Laundry.

Box.

A chair.

Not heroic.

Daily.

"What do I want to do?" I asked.

Tavi nodded.

"Carry soup."

I laughed.

"Why soup?"

"If spill, bad."

Correct.

High-fidelity task design by child.

Cala looked over from basin.

"Don't bring soup to leg shop."

"Thank you."

Tavi objected.

"They asked."

"They did not ask for soup."

"Real task."

I stared at him.

He had heard enough.

Dangerous household.

Lyssa came downstairs behind me.

"Carry a tray."

I turned.

"That's less funny."

"That's why."

A tray.

Two cups.

Maybe a bowl.

Weight low.

Hands occupied.

Walking surface visible.

Balance errors visible.

Actual household function.

Masta would approve.

Probably.

I wrote on bottom of her letter:

**REAL TASK: carry loaded tray across room without using hands for support.**

Then added:

**Only if Masta says safe.**

Hessa disease advanced.

Lyssa read over shoulder.

"Good."

Tavi said, "Soup."

"No soup."

"Water."

"Maybe."

"Two waters."

"Why two?"

"Harder."

Kid understood progression systems.

Terrible.

I packed.

Then did something strange.

Nothing.

No last-minute work board.

No trip financing scheme.

No attempt to turn Duskport into three commercial purposes because one city could theoretically hold several.

I had one purpose.

Fit.

Maybe two.

Come home.

That counted.

Afternoon passed.

Lyssa left for a customer fitting.

Cala went downstairs.

Tavi disappeared into courtyard with spoon machine.

I sat alone.

The Lakeward statement remained in records.

Did not move.

Duskport ticket stayed in notebook.

Did not become investment thesis.

I checked money once.

Not six times.

Still enough.

At evening Lyssa came back with fewer pins and more thread.

We ate.

I told her coach time.

She told me morning market would be loud because two grain carts were due.

Separate information.

Normal.

Before bed, I set liner on top of bag.

Then ticket under it.

Then moved ticket back to notebook because putting paper beneath padded leather was stupid.

Lyssa watched.

"Ready?"

"Mostly."

"Scared?"

I considered lying.

Not useful.

"A little."

"Walking?"

"Fitting."

She nodded.

"Because?"

"Last time my body kept making bad fit look better."

"That sounds like you."

"Everybody has one joke."

She smiled.

Then serious enough.

"You don't have to be good at it."

Masta had said walk honestly.

Lyssa said same thing differently.

Not mentor.

Not therapist.

Just person who had watched me turn being useful into religion more than once.

"I know."

This time I meant it.

Morning came.

I left on two crutches.

Not carrying a new leg.

Not carrying a debt.

Not carrying Lakeward.

One bag.

One liner.

One passenger ticket I had paid for because arriving useful was worth money.

At the coach yard, the freight wagon from yesterday was also loading.

Two men rolled hardware crates up plank.

For one second I regretted the silver.

Then one crate slipped sideways.

Not dangerous.

Caught immediately.

Still.

My shoulder remembered enough imaginary labor to shut up.

I boarded passenger coach.

Seat near aisle.

Bag under knees.

Crutches strapped to side rack where I could reach them.

The driver checked ticket.

"Destination?"

"Duskport."

"Work?"

"Client."

Word felt strange.

Not worker.

Not debtor.

Not patient exactly.

Client.

I had paid a shop to build something for my body.

I had paid a coach to bring that body there in useful condition.

That was enough job for one road.

The coach rolled east.

For the first hour I kept expecting somebody to hand me a crate.

Nobody did.

Passenger travel was deeply inefficient.

I sat.

A woman across from me knitted something red while the road moved under us. Beside her, a man with a merchant badge slept with both hands folded over a narrow brass case chained to his belt.

Interesting case.

Not mine.

I looked out the window.

Carrow flattened behind us.

Road widened past the east farms, then narrowed again where old stone drainage cuts climbed through low hills.

I knew some of this route.

Not all.

Forty years of old life did not make every ditch nostalgic.

At first stop, driver called fifteen minutes.

My right leg appreciated standing.

Shoulders fine.

Residual limb ordinary.

No fitting shell yet, just crutch body doing what it knew.

A freight handler nearby recognized the passenger coach and asked if anyone wanted two copper for moving sacks from one cart to another before departure.

My head turned automatically.

Two copper.

Easy.

Probably.

I looked at sacks.

Then at shoulders.

Then at ticket.

"No."

The handler shrugged and asked next person.

Nothing happened.

Excellent.

The world survived my refusal.

I bought water and a meat pastry instead.

Capital deployment.

Very advanced.

Back on coach, the knitting woman said, "You could've done that."

"Probably."

"Then why not?"

"Paying a woman in Duskport to tell me whether my body is lying."

She stopped knitting.

"Ah."

That was apparently sufficient explanation.

Good.

The brass-case man woke an hour later, checked chain, and went back to sleep.

I never learned what was inside.

Also good.

First overnight stop came at a road inn large enough to have three stables and no architectural interest in beauty.

The driver announced departure after first bell.

Floor space was cheap.

Beds were more.

I stood in doorway and had same argument with myself again.

A floor would not kill me.

I had slept on worse.

A floor also meant low transfers, bad shoulder angles, and waking stiff before another day in coach.

I paid for a bed.

Not expensive enough to deserve emotional accounting.

Expensive enough that early Greg would have called it weakness.

Current Greg called it sleeping.

The mattress was lumpy.

Financial independence had limits.

I slept anyway.

Morning body report:

Shoulders normal.

Right hip stiff for maybe ten steps.

Residual limb skin clean.

No swelling worth naming.

Good.

I wrote none of that down.

Masta had not asked for a travel diary.

The second day changed landscape.

More wet ground.

More old industrial cuts.

By afternoon, Duskport began announcing itself through smell before buildings.

Wet metal.

River mud.

Smoke.

Work.

I had missed none of those things.

Still recognized all of them.

The city came into view under low cloud.

Warehouses first.

Then cranes.

Then roofs.

No revelation.

Just place.

That mattered more now.

I had lived here long enough for some corners to exist in body memory.

Coach entered west terminal after fourth bell.

Driver unstrapped my crutches.

"Client," he said.

I looked at him.

"What?"

"Your destination answer."

"Oh."

"Hope it fits."

There.

Random stranger had now joined project.

"Me too."

I stepped down.

Duskport under crutches felt familiar immediately.

Different stone spacing than Carrow.

Wider freight lanes.

More people who expected you to move with traffic instead of around it.

I moved.

Anchor's End still existed.

Good.

I paid posted room rate without interrogating desk clerk about cheapest possible alternative.

This was getting dangerous.

Bag upstairs.

Liner on top.

Then I went outside.

Hark & Venn was three streets away.

I knew that.

My appointment was not today.

Also knew that.

I walked one street toward it anyway.

Stopped.

This was stupid.

Not illegal.

Different category.

Masta had fitting space three days from now.

Showing up early would not make shell more ready.

Could ask whether she had cancellation.

Could also become man who turned other people's schedule into his enthusiasm.

No.

I turned toward market instead.

Not artifact market.

Food.

Mostly.

Duskport had enough old hardware in every second stall that "not artifact market" was philosophical.

I bought dinner.

Saw one retired signal clamp with a bead still in it.

Did not ask price.

Saw a broken tide lens with maker mark I almost recognized.

Almost.

Kept walking.

Three days.

I could work if useful.

Could visit people if natural.

Could do nothing if nothing needed me.

That last option remained suspicious.

At Anchor's End that evening, I wrote Masta one reply even though I was already in city.

**ARRIVED. FITTING WINDOW CONFIRMED. LINER WITH ME. REAL TASK: LOADED TRAY, IF YOU APPROVE. I WILL NOT ARRIVE EARLY AND HAUNT YOUR SHOP.**

I paid a boy one bit to deliver it tomorrow morning.

Then added after thought:

**NO SOUP.**

Tavi deserved representation.

I folded note.

For once I had arrived somewhere before the problem.

No job attached.

No debt attached.

No emergency.

Three days until fitting.

Enough money to sleep in a bed.

Enough sense not to spend the night proving I deserved it.

That was probably what being a client felt like.

Annoyingly passive.

Potentially useful.

I could survive three days.

Probably.
